structure.overview: Mr. Smeele applied for judicial review of a CRA Officer's decision denying his eligibility for the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) due to not meeting the $5,000 income threshold from self-employment in 2019 or 2020. The CRA found his Airbnb and car rental income to be rental income rather than self-employment income, a finding the court found reasonable. The court dismissed Mr. Smeele's application for judicial review, finding no reviewable error in the Officer's decision.

sections.label: CRA's income assessment and CRB eligibility decisions
Analysis of income classification and evidence
Consideration of additional arguments and burden of proof

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Applicant Mr. Smeele seeks judicial review of CRA Officer's decision denying CRB eligibility due to not meeting $5000 income threshold in 2019 or 2020.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court expresses sympathy for Mr. Smeele but finds no reviewable error in Officer's decision and will dismiss the application.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: CRB introduced Sept 26, 2020; Mr. Smeele applied Oct 12, 2020, received payments for seven periods; file selected for eligibility review Jan 12, 2021.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele submitted documents showing $7,400+ Airbnb and car rental income in 2019 but initially reported a net loss; he applied to amend tax return to report $5,236 net self-employment income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: First Reviewer denied CRB on Aug 5, 2021, finding Mr. Smeele did not meet income threshold or 50% income reduction requirement under the Act.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Second Reviewer in Oct-Nov 2021 denied CRB, ruling Airbnb and car rental income was rental income, not self-employment income, thus not meeting threshold.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele discontinued judicial review after CRA agreed to third review; he submitted new documents including an archived CRA bulletin on rental property income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele submitted affidavits describing extra services provided to Airbnb guests to argue income was self-employment income, not rental income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Third-level Officer refused CRB on Mar 18, 2022, again finding income was rental income; breakdown showed host and cleaning fees totaling less than $6000.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer concluded host and cleaning fees alone did not meet $5000 threshold; no other income breakdown provided; Mr. Smeele did not qualify for CRB.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Attorney General requested style of cause be amended to name Attorney General as respondent; court agrees and will order amendment.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Issue is whether Officer reasonably found Mr. Smeele ineligible for CRB due to income threshold; standard of review is reasonableness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele bases review on facts and arguments not before Officer; issue before CRA was whether Airbnb income was self-employment or rental income.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele argued Airbnb income was self-employment based on CRA bulletin; provided evidence of fees and affidavits describing extra services.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Officer found Airbnb income was rental income despite extra services and considered the CRA bulletin; this finding is accepted by court.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Before court, Mr. Smeele raised new argument about $6,000 art sale in 2019 not included in income; affidavit provided but no bank proof; inconsistency in sale date noted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court explains it must assess Officer's decision based on information before Officer; new arguments not before Officer cannot make decision unreasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele reasserted Airbnb income was self-employment based on bulletin and extra services; Officer found services insufficient to reclassify income; court finds this reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Only monetary breakdown for extra services was hosting and cleaning fees totaling less than $5,000, below minimum income threshold.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele's partner, Ms. Pemberton-Smith, argued the Airbnb was a true business creating an artist space, not just a side investment.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court notes Ms. Pemberton-Smith's broader business vision was not before Officer; Officer only had minimal evidence of extra services and found income was rental.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court states if broader business model had been submitted, Officer's decision might differ; burden is on claimant; Officer not obliged to make claimant's case.
idea_list: No duty to make claimant's case

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Application for judicial review is dismissed; no costs awarded.
